title: Variables, Constants & Literals
html:
A variable is a named, typed region of memory. C gives you three kinds of constants: literals, const objects, and #define / enum names.

Declaring and initialising

Watch out

Local (automatic) variables are not initialised — their initial value is garbage and reading it is undefined behaviour. Globals and static variables are zero-initialised.

Identifier rules

  • Letters, digits and _; cannot start with a digit; case-sensitive (count ≠ Count).
  • Cannot be a keyword (int, return, static, sizeof…).
  • Names starting with _ + uppercase letter or __ are reserved for the implementation — don’t use them.
  • Convention: snake_case for variables and functions, UPPER_CASE for macros and constants.

Literals

LiteralTypeExample
Decimal / octal / hex integerint (or larger if needed)42, 052, 0x2A
Suffixes u, l, llunsigned, long, long long42u, 42L, 42ULL
Floatingdouble by default3.14, 1e-3, 2.5f (float), 2.5L (long double)
Characterint (!)'A', '\n', '\0', '\x41'
Stringchar[N] (array incl. NUL)"hi" has 3 bytes
Compound (C99)unnamed object(int[]){1, 2, 3}
Watch out

A leading 0 makes an integer literal octal: 010 is 8, and 09 is a compile error.

Three ways to name a constant

FormExampleTyped?ScopeNotes
#define#define MAX 100NoFrom definition to end of fileText substitution by the preprocessor; no address
constconst int max = 100;YesBlock / fileA read-only variable; not a constant expression in C (can’t size a global array)
enumenum { MAX = 100 };intBlock / fileA true integer constant expression, visible to the debugger
What is the difference between #define and const?

#define is a preprocessor text replacement: no type, no scope, no storage, invisible to the debugger, and prone to precedence surprises. const creates a typed, scoped, read-only object with an address. In C (unlike C++) a const int is not a constant expression, so enum or #define is still used for array sizes and case labels.

What value does an uninitialised variable have?

Objects with static storage duration (globals, static locals) are zero-initialised. Automatic locals have an indeterminate value; reading it is undefined behaviour, which is why compilers warn (-Wuninitialized).
